meta.title: Investments in debt securities
meta.summary: Why companies invest, classifying debt securities as held-to-maturity, available-for-sale or trading, amortized cost and the effective-interest method, fair value adjustments through OCI or net income, sales and reclassification, credit losses and transfers.

videos.title: Classifying debt investments
videos.take: Debt securities are held-to-maturity, available-for-sale or trading, depending on intent and ability

scenes.say: After the IPO, Bluestem has more cash than it needs for the winter. It invests some in bonds.

scenes.heading: Why companies invest
items: Earn a return on idle cash
scenes.say: Companies invest to earn a return on idle cash, to line up cash for future needs like a plant expansion, or strategically, to influence or control another company. Strategic stakes are equity investments, next lecture.

scenes.heading: Three categories for debt securities
scenes.say: Debt securities fall into three categories. Held-to-maturity securities are carried at amortized cost. Available-for-sale securities are carried at fair value, with unrealized gains and losses in OCI. Trading securities are at fair value, with gains and losses in net income.
Held-to-maturity requires both the positive intent and the ability to hold the bonds until they mature. Selling them early can taint the whole category.
Trading securities are bought and held mainly to sell in the near term, as a bank's trading desk does. Available-for-sale is the residual: neither held-to-maturity nor trading.

scenes.q: Unrealized gains on available-for-sale debt securities are reported in:
scenes.say: Quick check. Unrealized gains on available-for-sale debt securities are reported where? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Held-to-maturity: amortized cost
videos.take: Record at cost; interest revenue = carrying amount × market rate; fair value changes are ignored

scenes.say: On January 1, 2030, Bluestem buys $500,000 of five-year, six percent bonds issued by a utility, paying interest semiannually. Similar bonds yield eight percent.

scenes.heading: Purchase price: 10 periods at 4%
scenes.say: Ten periods at four percent: the principal is worth $337,780 and the interest $121,664. Bluestem pays $459,444, a discount from face.

scenes.heading: Purchase
scenes.say: It records Debt Investments at cost, $459,444. Bluestem intends and is able to hold the bonds to maturity.

scenes.heading: June 30: first interest
scenes.say: On June 30, interest revenue is four percent of the carrying amount, $18,378. Cash received is $15,000. The $3,378 difference increases the investment to $462,822. It's the mirror of what an issuer does.
For held-to-maturity securities, changes in fair value aren't recognized, because Bluestem will collect the contractual cash flows. Fair value is disclosed in the notes.

scenes.q: HTM bond carrying amount $96,000; market rate 5% per period; cash interest $4,000. Interest revenue?
scenes.say: Quick check. A held-to-maturity bond's carrying amount is ninety-six thousand; market rate five percent per period; cash interest four thousand. Interest revenue? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Available-for-sale: fair value through OCI
videos.take: Amortize as usual, then adjust to fair value at year-end with the change in OCI

scenes.say: Suppose Bluestem might sell the utility bonds if it needs cash for the second plant. Then they're available-for-sale.

scenes.heading: December 31, 2030
scenes.say: Interest revenue and amortization are recorded exactly as before. After two periods, amortized cost is $466,335. At December 31, the bonds' fair value is $470,000: an unrealized holding gain of $3,665.

scenes.heading: Fair value adjustment
rows: Unrealized holding gain or loss, equity
scenes.say: Bluestem debits a Fair Value Adjustment account, which sits alongside the investment at amortized cost, and credits Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss, Equity: other comprehensive income.

scenes.heading: On the statements
scenes.say: The balance sheet shows the investment at fair value, $470,000. Net income includes interest revenue of $36,891 for the year. The $3,665 gain goes to other comprehensive income and accumulates in equity.

sub: Keeps unrealized swings out of income
scenes.say: Why OCI? Bluestem isn't trying to profit from short-term price changes, so putting the swings in net income could mislead. OCI shows them without distorting operating results.

scenes.q: AFS debt securities: amortized cost $210,000; fair value $203,000. The adjustment:
scenes.say: Quick check. Available-for-sale debt securities: amortized cost two ten thousand; fair value two oh three thousand. The adjustment? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, a $7,000 unrealized loss in OCI, unless it's a credit loss.

videos.title: Trading securities
videos.take: Trading securities are at fair value with unrealized gains and losses in net income

scenes.say: Maria Okafor sets up a small treasury account that actively trades short-term corporate bonds.

scenes.heading: Trading portfolio, December 31
scenes.say: The portfolio cost $200,000 and is worth $194,000 at year-end: an unrealized holding loss of $6,000.

scenes.heading: Adjusting to fair value
scenes.say: For trading securities, the loss goes straight into net income. Trading securities are usually current assets, and interest revenue is recorded as earned; amortization of small discounts is often skipped.

scenes.heading: Same price drop, three results
scenes.say: The same price drop has three different results. Held-to-maturity: no change. Available-for-sale: fair value on the balance sheet, loss in OCI. Trading: fair value and a loss in net income.
Because classification changes income, auditors test management's intent against its actual behavior. A company that regularly sells HTM bonds loses the right to use the category.

scenes.q: Trading securities: cost $80,000; fair value $86,000. Effect on net income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Trading securities: cost eighty thousand; fair value eighty-six thousand. Effect on net income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Selling AFS securities and credit losses
videos.take: On sale, reclassify accumulated OCI into net income; credit losses go to income through an allowance

scenes.say: In 2031, Bluestem sells the utility bonds to fund the second plant.

scenes.heading: Sale on January 2, 2031
scenes.say: It sells the bonds for $471,000. The realized gain is measured against amortized cost: $4,665, reported in net income.

The $3,665 gain already in OCI must be removed, or it would be counted twice in comprehensive income: once in OCI last year, and again in this year's realized gain. That's a reclassification adjustment, or recycling.

scenes.heading: Credit losses on debt investments
items: HTM: CECL allowance for expected losses
AFS: allowance, limited to fair value shortfall
Credit losses go to net income
scenes.say: Credit losses are different. For held-to-maturity bonds, Bluestem records an allowance for expected credit losses under CECL. For available-for-sale bonds, credit losses go to income through an allowance, limited to the amount fair value is below amortized cost. Non-credit declines stay in OCI.
The key distinction: if prices fell because interest rates rose, that's OCI for AFS. If they fell because the issuer may not pay, that's a credit loss in income.

scenes.q: AFS bonds with amortized cost $100,000 and $2,000 unrealized gain in AOCI are sold for $103,000. Realized gain in net income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Available-for-sale bonds with amortized cost one hundred thousand and a two thousand dollar unrealized gain in AOCI are sold for one oh three thousand. Realized gain in net income? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $3,000. The $2,000 in AOCI is reclassified.

videos.title: Transfers and disclosures
videos.take: Transfers between categories are at fair value; disclose fair values, maturities and gains and losses

scenes.say: What if Bluestem changes its mind about a bond's category?

scenes.heading: Transfers between categories
rows: Unrealized gain or loss to OCI
scenes.say: Transfers are made at fair value. Moving to trading recognizes any unrealized gain or loss in income right away. Moving from held-to-maturity to available-for-sale puts the unrealized amount in OCI. Moving available-for-sale to held-to-maturity amortizes the OCI amount over the remaining life.
Transfers should be rare, especially into or out of trading, because intent is supposed to be stable.

scenes.heading: Disclosures
items: Amortized cost and fair value by type
Proceeds and realized gains on sales
scenes.say: Notes disclose amortized cost and fair value by type of security, maturities, gross unrealized gains and losses, sales proceeds and realized gains, and the fair value hierarchy levels used.

sub: Any debt security may be elected:
scenes.say: Companies may also elect the fair value option for any debt security, reporting all changes in net income, much like trading.

scenes.q: An AFS bond with $4,000 of unrealized gain in AOCI is transferred to trading. The $4,000:
opts: Is recognized in net income now
scenes.say: Quick check. An available-for-sale bond with four thousand of unrealized gain in AOCI is transferred to trading. What happens to the four thousand? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, it's recognized in net income now.

warmup: Bluestem buys a utility bond and its price drops 3% because interest rates rose. Has Bluestem lost money? What if it holds the bond to maturity?
Depends on intent: HTM collects contractual cash; sets up classification.
acts: Classify: (a) bonds bought to fund a plant in 4 years, may sell if needed; (b) bonds the treasury desk trades weekly; (c) bonds Bluestem will hold to maturity and can afford to.
Bluestem buys $200,000 of 4-year, 5% bonds (semiannual) to yield 6% (8 periods at 3%: PV of 1 0.78941; PVA 7.01969). Price and first interest entry (HTM).
AFS: amortized cost $194,582; fair value $191,000. Record the adjustment. Next year, amortized cost $196,250 and fair value $199,000: record.
Year 1: unrealized loss 3,582 in OCI (FVA credit 3,582). Year 2: required FVA debit 2,750; adjust by 6,332.
Trading portfolio: cost $120,000; fair value $126,500. Record. Next year it's sold for $124,000.
Gain 6,500 in NI; on sale, loss 2,500 vs fair value carrying amount.
AFS bonds: amortized cost $300,000; AOCI unrealized loss $8,000; sold for $295,000. Record the realized loss and reclassification.
Realized loss 5,000 in NI; reclassify 8,000 out of OCI (fair value adjustment eliminated).
An AFS bond's fair value fell $20,000 below amortized cost: $12,000 due to rising rates and $8,000 due to expected credit loss. Report each part.
Credit loss 8,000 to NI via allowance; 12,000 to OCI.
case: Bluestem holds three bond portfolios at December 31, 2030: (A) $459,444 cost utility bonds, amortized cost $466,335, fair value $470,000; (B) a trading portfolio, cost $200,000, fair value $194,000; (C) Treasury notes held to maturity, amortized cost $150,000, fair value $146,000. The founder wants to classify everything as HTM 'to keep income stable', but Bluestem expects to sell A to fund the plant.
Report each portfolio and its income and OCI effects.
What happens to income if B were reclassified as AFS?

A (AFS): 470,000; OCI gain 3,665. B (trading): 194,000; loss 6,000 in NI. C (HTM): 150,000; FV disclosed. A can't be HTM: Bluestem expects to sell it. B to AFS would move the 6,000 to OCI, but transfers out of trading must be rare and justified; trading intent drives classification. Proposal misrepresents intent; auditors would challenge.
